Chapter 8: The Mirror—Parenting, Vulnerability, and the Fear of Repeating the Past.
Becoming a parent can feel like reaching a huge turning point. But if you’ve grown up with trauma, it’s more like standing on the edge of a cliff, heart racing, wondering what comes next. Imagine this man—he’s now got a child of his own, and suddenly, all those old fears he thought he’d left behind? They come roaring back.
Every little decision—how do you discipline? How do you comfort? How do you just show love?—starts to feel like a test. Will you repeat the same mistakes your parents made, or can you find a new way forward?
He looks at his child with this mix of amazement and, honestly, a little bit of fear. There’s so much innocence, so much trust and pure joy. It’s everything he missed out on as a kid. All he wants is to protect that light, to give his child the safety he never had. But let’s be real—old habits are tough to shake. Sometimes, when life gets stressful, he can feel that old anger bubbling up, sharp and unexpected. His heart pounds as he catches himself, worried about what he might become in those moments.
Doubt creeps in. Is he doing enough? Is he making the right choices? The fear of failing, of causing harm—it never really goes away. But here’s something important: he notices the power of just being aware. He learns to pause, to take a breath, to react differently. And when he slips up—and he does, because all parents do—he apologizes. He shows his child that it’s okay to be imperfect, that mistakes are part of being human.
Parenting becomes a kind of mirror. It reflects all the pain from the past, but also the hope for something better. He starts to realize that being vulnerable isn’t a weakness—it’s actually a strength. By opening up about his struggles in ways his child can understand, he’s teaching honesty and resilience. He’s showing that big feelings are normal and safe, that you can mess up and still be loved.
The fear of repeating the past never fully disappears. But over time, it loses its grip. Every day becomes a chance to choose kindness, to build trust, to make new, happier memories. Healing, he discovers, isn’t just about his own journey—it’s about breaking the cycle for his child. He finds hope in small moments: bedtime stories, shared laughter, quiet hugs. These are the pieces that start to build a new kind of childhood.
As he looks at his child, he realizes something powerful. The scars of his past don’t have to define the future. With love, patience, and a bit of courage, he can help write a whole new story—one built on trust, vulnerability, and real, lasting connection.
